items.description:
Microsoft Dev Box will
retire on September 18, 2028. Beginning on September 14, 2026,
Microsoft Dev Box will begin the closing-down process. After retirement,
Microsoft Dev Box will no longer be available. Microsoft Dev Box is currently in maintenance mode, and
Microsoft’s investments for developer cloud environments are focused on Windows
365. Existing Microsoft Dev Box usage remains supported during the transition
period, and we recommend that you begin planning your migration now to avoid
disruption to developer workflows. What this means for you If
you currently use Microsoft Dev Box, you can continue using your existing
deployments during the transition period. No
new feature development is planned for the service. You
should evaluate and begin planning your move to Windows 365, which is
the recommended path forward for virtualized developer environments. Recommended action Review
your current Dev Box usage, including dev centers, projects, pools, images, and
developer workflows. Identify
which scenarios can transition directly to Windows 365 and which require
additional planning. Validate
identity, device management, networking, image, and licensing requirements for
your future-state environment. Begin
testing replacement workflows as early as possible to reduce risk before
retirement.  If you have questions or need support, please contact your
Microsoft representative.
items.title: Retirement: Microsoft Dev Box will be retired on September 18, 2028

items.description:
Azure Deployment
Environments will retire on February 22, 2027. Beginning on September
14, 2026, Azure Deployment Environments will begin the closing-down
process. After retirement, the service will no longer be available. To help avoid disruption, we recommend that you begin
assessing your current usage and planning your transition now. Review the
environments, templates, and workflows in your organization that depend on
Azure Deployment Environments and identify the replacement approach that best
supports your requirements. What this means for you You
should review all current Azure Deployment Environments usage across
subscriptions, projects, templates, and deployment workflows. You
should identify an alternative approach for environment provisioning and
developer self-service before the retirement date. You
should begin validating your migration plan as early as possible to minimize
operational and development impact. Recommended action Inventory
your current environments, templates, catalogs, and provisioning workflows. Determine
the target platform or service that will replace Azure Deployment Environments
for your organization. Test
your migration path, including governance, access control,
infrastructure-as-code compatibility, and developer workflow readiness. Communicate
internal timelines to platform engineering teams, developers, and
administrators.
items.title: Retirement: Azure Deployment Environments will be retired on February 22, 2027

items.description:
Azure App Service on Azure Stack Hub will be retired on September
30, 2029. Starting September 30, 2026, new installations will
no longer be supported, and no new product releases, features, or enhancements
will be made available. Existing supported deployments can continue to run and
upgrade to the latest available release until retirement. Customers should begin planning migration to Azure App
Service in Azure now to continue receiving support, security updates, platform improvements,
and new capabilities. On September 30th, 2029, App Service on
Azure Stack will reach retirement and Microsoft support will end. Recommended action  Assessand migrate applications as soon as possible. Azure
App Service in Azure provides a fully managed platform with global availability,
Windows and Linux hosting options, autoscale, deployment slots, advanced
networking and security, Azure services integration, and continuous innovation. For applications with complex Windows dependencies, evaluate
Managed Instance on Azure App Service. It can help accelerate migration for
applications requiring registry access, COM components, custom runtimes, or
other Windows-specific dependencies. For a successful transition, inventory applications and
dependencies, assess compatibility, select the appropriate Azure hosting
target, migrate code, configuration, and data, validate workloads, and complete
migration before September 30, 2029. Learn more:  Benefits Plan Migrate
items.title: Retirement: Azure App Service on Azure Stack Hub

items.description: Always Encrypted with Intel SGX enclaves in Azure SQL Database will retire on October 31, 2027 as support for SGX-enabled DC-series hardware is phased out. Customers should transition to Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) enclaves, a hardware-independent alternative, or consider SQL Server on Confidential VMs.Customer impactAfter retirement, workloads using Intel SGX enclaves will no longer have enclave functionality. Databases running on DC-series compute tiers should be migrated to supported compute tiers to continue using enclave-enabled features.Recommended actionsMigrate from DC-series to a supported Standard-series (non-DC) compute tier.Enable VBS enclaves for Always Encrypted. No attestation is required.Update client drivers to versions that support VBS enclaves.Update connection strings to remove SGX attestation parameters and use VBS enclave mode.We recommend planning and validating your migration well in advance of the retirement date to ensure a smooth transition.
items.title: Retirement: Always Encrypted with Intel SGX Enclaves

items.description:
Beginning September 30, 2027, support for the pod name dimension on the following Azure
Monitor platform metrics is retiring, and these metrics are transitioning to aggregate pod counters:Number of pods by phase (kube_pod_status_phase)Number of pods in Ready state (kube_pod_status_ready)After this change:Metric names remain unchanged.Aggregate pod counts remain available.Namespace-level monitoring scenarios remain supported.The pod name dimension will no longer be available for filtering, grouping, or alerting.During the deprecation period, AKS will maintain both the existing and the new aggregate implementations. Both are populated with data, existing monitoring experiences will continue to function, and you will have at least one year of historical data in the aggregate implementation before retirement.You may be affected if any dashboard, workbook, alert, automation, or monitoring workflow:Uses kube_pod_status_phase or kube_pod_status_ready and filters on the pod name dimension.Splits or groups results by the pod name dimension.Recommended action: If you use aggregate pod counts, no action is required.If you use the pod name dimension, update dashboards, alerts, workbooks, and automation before September 30, 2027. For pod-level monitoring and troubleshooting, we recommend using Azure
Monitor Managed Prometheus and Kubernetes-native
pod metrics.Help and supportIf you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A.

items.description: The Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes will be retired on October 9, 2027.Customers currently using the extension should plan to migrate to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension before the retirement date. The Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension provides equivalent functionality for accessing and synchronizing secrets from Azure Key Vault for workloads running on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters. In addition, the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension includes enhancements such as support for offline access to secrets and authentication using workload identity federation, enabling applications to access Azure Key Vault without storing long-lived credentials on the cluster.After retirement, the Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension will no longer receive new features, bug fixes, security updates, or technical support.Migration guidance is available to help customers transition their workloads and configurations to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension ahead of retirement.
items.title: Retirement: Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension for Azure Arc enabled Kubernetes clusters

items.description:
Standard service endpoint, a
new capability in the Azure Private Link family, provides a scalable and secure
approach for connecting Azure IaaS workloads to Azure PaaS services. Standard service
endpoint addresses the manageability, and the scale limitations of traditional
service endpoints by using Public IP addresses as network identifiers and
integrating with network security perimeter. This enables organizations to
achieve large-scale IaaS-to-PaaS connectivity while maintaining strong network
access controls and simplified operations. With standard service endpoint,
customers can associate a public IP instance with multiple subnets and virtual
networks across subscriptions within the same tenant and region. When combined
with network security perimeter, organizations can create a logical security
boundary around supported Azure services, including Azure Storage, Azure SQL
Database, Azure Cosmos DB, and Azure Key Vault. Access can then be restricted
so that only approved networks and workloads are allowed to communicate with
these resources, helping reduce operational complexity while strengthening
security posture. Standard service endpoint is a
paid Azure feature and is billed at a fixed rate per virtual network (VNet) per
hour. Learn more: Documentation  Azure
Private Link pricing
items.title: Generally Available: Standard service endpoint

items.description: MVUs are now available for elastic clusters in Azure Database for PostgreSQL. You can upgrade an existing elastic cluster to a supported newer PostgreSQL version in place without provisioning a replacement cluster, migrating distributed data, or changing your application connection endpoint. This managed upgrade experience helps reduce the downtime, complexity, and operational effort associated with traditional migration-based upgrades. You can use MVUs to keep distributed PostgreSQL workloads on supported versions and adopt the latest PostgreSQL and Citus performance improvements, capabilities, and security updates. By extending the Flexible Server upgrade experience to elastic clusters, you can manage the version lifecycle of sharded workloads more efficiently while retaining your existing cluster topology and configuration. Learn more.
items.title: Public Preview:  Major version upgrades (MVU) for Azure Database for PostgreSQL elastic clusters

items.description:
The public preview of Microsoft-managed performance monitoring for SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines is now available. You can now monitor SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines without building custom collection scripts or correlating telemetry across disconnected tools. The SQL IaaS Agent extension collects performance data from your SQL Server instances and sends it to a Microsoft-managed telemetry pipeline for processing and storage. Resource-level and estate-wide dashboards help you identify performance trends, anomalies, and resource bottlenecks. Integration with Fabric Database Hub brings this telemetry into a unified monitoring experience. For deeper analysis and custom visualizations, you can securely query your data with Kusto Query Language through an RBAC-protected Azure Data Explorer proxy endpoint. Learn more:  
 Documentation  
 Announcement
     blog
products: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

items.description:
As part of the Microsoft Azure VM lifecycle
policy, Microsoft is announcing the retirement of the Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and
Esv3 Azure VM series in public cloud Azure regions. These VMs will enter the
End-of-Life lifecycle stage and retire on November 15, 2029. We know migrating production workloads takes planning and
engineering time. To keep your applications and workloads running without
interruption, migrate any Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, or Esv3 series VMs to a newer VM
series before November 15, 2029. After this date, Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3
virtual machines will enter the Retired lifecycle stage and will no longer be
supported on Azure. Virtual machines not transitioned by that time may be
deallocated and ultimately deleted as the underlying hardware and platform
infrastructure are retired. We recommend evaluating available modernization
options as soon as possible and moving to newer VM generations, such as Azure
Dsv5 or Esv5v5 series virtual machines, to maintain uninterrupted service and
gain improved performance, security, and reliability.  Additionally, as previously
communicated, as of July 1, 2026, one-year and three-year Reserved
Instances (RIs) for the Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 VM series are no
longer available for purchase or renewal. If you would like to continue
commitment savings, we recommend reviewing your current
reserved instance orders and if RIs are still in effect for these
VMs, consider a trade-in
of active reservations for Azure
savings plan for compute contracts.   Help and support   Microsoft is committed to ensuring every customer navigates
this transition quickly, successfully, and with clarity. Customers with an
active support plan can submit a support
request for technical assistance with migration planning and execution. For
general questions, Microsoft
Q&A provides access to community experts.  Learn more:   
 Azure Virtual
     Machines Lifecycle policy  
 v5 modernization
     guide   
 Modernize
     to the v6 and v7 VM series - Azure Virtual Machines
items.title: Retirement: Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 Azure VMs

items.description: Azure Backup for PostgreSQL flexible server and elastic cluster (v2) preview brings enterprise-grade long-term retention to PostgreSQL. Backups are taken as physical backups from managed disk snapshots and vaulted in an Azure Backup vault, so protection now extends to servers of up to 32 TB on Premium SSD v1 and up to 64 TB on Premium SSD v2. The first backup is full and every backup after it is incremental, which keeps daily protection practical at multi-terabyte scale, with a recovery point objective goal of one day and retention configurable from 7 days up to 10 years.The v1 solution took logical backups, which capped server size at 1 TB, allowed a single vaulted backup each week, produced full copies every time, and returned data as files that had to be imported by hand before it could be used. Physical backups lift those constraints together, extend protection to elastic cluster as well as flexible server, and introduce Restore as Server.The preview includes the following capabilities:Backup for both PostgreSQL flexible server and elastic cluster.Servers of up to 32 TB on Premium SSD v1 and up to 64 TB on Premium SSD v2.Daily and weekly schedules, along with on-demand backups.Incremental backups after the first full backup, with a recovery point objective goal of one day.Restore as Server onto a pre-created flexible server or elastic cluster, with no intermediate storage account and no manual import.Retention up to 10 years with independent daily, weekly, monthly and yearly rules, protected by vault soft delete, immutability, Multi-user authorization and Customer Managed Key encryption.Support for WORM immutable backups, so that recovery points cannot be altered or deleted before their retention period expires.Billing will be enabled from October 15, 2026.  Learn more: Documentation   Azure Backup pricing Pricing calculator
items.title: Public Preview: Azure Backup for PostgreSQL flexible server and elastic cluster (v2)

items.description:
Starting with SQL Server 2025 CU9 and SQL Server 2022 CU27, SQL Server on Linux supports the bulkadmin fixed server role and the ADMINISTER BULK OPERATIONS permission for performing bulk data import operations without requiring users to be members of the sysadmin fixed server role. This capability enables you to use operations such as BULK INSERT and OPENROWSET(BULK...) while following a least-privilege security model. Previously on SQL Server on Linux, these operations required sysadmin membership.With this release, organizations running SQL Server on Linux can provide users with the permissions required for bulk data loading without granting broader sysadmin privileges, improving alignment with the principle of least privilege. The feature applies to SQL Server on Linux, including on-premises, SQL Server on Azure VMs and container deployments.Learn
more.
items.title: Generally Available: Enabling the Bulk admin role for SQL Server on Linux

items.description: Anyscale on Azure is now Generally Available. Anyscale on Azure is a managed platform for running distributed Python workloads on Ray. It deploys directly onto your Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster and integrates with the Azure services your team already uses. Unlike other processing engines which either only support one hardware type (e.g. CPUs) or focus on a single workload (e.g. inference), Ray turns a heterogeneous cluster of CPUs and GPUs into a single Python runtime composing data preparation, distributed training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, high-throughput inference, and agentic execution as one program. Anyscale on Azure brings Ray, the distributed compute runtime,  into your Azure tenant as an Azure Native service, that includes purpose-built developer tooling and unified pane for cluster management, built through deep engineering collaboration between Anyscale and Microsoft.
items.title: Generally Available: Anyscale on Azure

items.description:
Running Kubernetes on-premises often means adding a
virtualization layer, adapting to unfamiliar infrastructure, or giving up
control over the hardware and software your applications depend on. For AI
workloads, these tradeoffs can limit access to local data, reduce available
compute capacity, and restrict your choice of GPUs, drivers, and runtimes.AKS on bare metal
Ubuntu, now in public preview, brings the AKS experience directly to customer
owned Ubuntu infrastructure. Deploy a complete Kubernetes cluster on your hardware
using Azure CLI. Choose the CPU and GPU hardware and supporting software stack
that fit your workloads.Run applications close to your data, dedicate more
infrastructure capacity to your workloads, and manage Kubernetes through
familiar AKS and Azure workflows. You keep the flexibility of Ubuntu and your
hardware while extending a consistent AKS operating model to your on-premises
environment.Learn more.
items.title: Public Preview: AKS on bare metal now on Ubuntu

items.description:
Announcing the Public Preview of IPv6 support for Application Gateway WAF.Application Gateway Web Application Firewall (WAF) now supports inspection and enforcement for IPv6 traffic in Public Preview, marking a major step forward in modernizing the platform for dual‑stack environments. As IPv6 adoption accelerates globally due to IPv4 exhaustion and modern connectivity requirements, this enhancement enables customers to embrace IPv6 without compromising their security posture.With this update, Application Gateway WAF extends its full protection stack -including managed rule sets, custom rules, and diagnostics - to IPv6 traffic. Customers operating dual‑stack applications can now apply consistent security controls across both IPv4 and IPv6. Additionally, IPv6 geo‑based custom rules are available through AFEC enrollment, providing more granular traffic governance during the preview.Learn
more.
items.title: Public Preview: IPv6 Support for Application Gateway WAF

items.description: Starting October 15, 2026, Search in Microsoft Fabric will return tables from semantic models, lakehouses, and mirrored databases as individual results. Users can search by table name or description, or find a table by an exact column-name match.  More object types will become available over time. This applies to Fabric's global search, the OneLake Catalog UI, the Search API, search in Fabric's MCP servers, the /find command in the Fabric CLI, and the discovery skill.What you need to know: Table visibility in search follows permissions on the parent item, not data-level permissions on the table. If a user has Read permission or higher on the item, they can discover all tables under that item, even tables they can't query. Search does not grant access to table data; existing data-access controls still apply when a user opens or queries a table. Tables in semantic models protected by object-level security are excluded from search. Action: Review "Users can find objects in search" setting in the Fabric admin portal under Tenant settings. It's enabled by default. Turn it off if your organization isn't ready for users to find tables by search; item and data access won't change.
items.title: Announcing: Table discovery in OneLake Catalog search

items.description: The integration between Microsoft Agent 365 and Azure API Management is now available in public preview, helping organizations connect centralized governance with runtime enforcement for MCP servers and tools.With this integration, organizations can:Discover Azure API Management gateways and MCP servers in Agent 365, creating a centralized inventory of gateway-managed tools.Control access to MCP servers from Agent 365, with enforcement applied by Azure API Management at runtime.Apply tool-level access controls with the Azure API Management AI Gateway tier, including blocking individual tools without disabling the entire MCP server.Monitor tool activity to support auditing, operational visibility, and incident investigation.Protect tool interactions using Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Purview capabilities to evaluate tool requests and responses for security threats and sensitive-information risks.Azure API Management v2 tiers support centralized MCP inventory and server-level blocking and unblocking. The AI Gateway tier, currently in preview, adds individual tool-level blocking, tool activity observability, and tool threat protection.This integration enables AI administrators to manage governance centrally in Agent 365 while platform teams enforce those policies through Azure API Management in the customer’s Azure environment.
items.title: Public Preview: Microsoft Agent 365 integration with Azure API Management

items.description:
External key management for Azure Key Vault Managed HSM is now generally available in all Azure public regions. For organizations with regulatory or sovereignty requirements to retain physical control of key-encryption keys, it lets Azure services that support customer-managed keys with Managed HSM use keys held in a customer-operated hardware security module (HSM) outside Microsoft infrastructure. Managed HSM delegates key wrap and unwrap operations through a customer-operated proxy; the external key material stays outside Microsoft infrastructure.Access requires enablement through your Microsoft account team. Connectivity to the proxy over the public internet is available with the GA feature. Azure Private Link integration is in public preview. Customers or their HSM providers are responsible for the external HSM, proxy, and network availability; these components are outside the Managed HSM service-level agreement (SLA).Learn
more.
items.title: Generally Available: External key management for Azure Key Vault Managed HSM

items.description:
Announcing the general availability of exceptions
for Web Application Firewall on Azure Application Gateway and Azure Front Door.Azure Web
Application Firewall (WAF) helps protect your web applications from common
threats and attacks. In some cases, WAF may block requests that are safe and
expected for your application. Existing exclusions help reduce false positives
by omitting specific request attributes, such as headers, cookies, query string
arguments, or body fields, from WAF evaluation while the rest of the request
continues to be inspected. Exceptions
provide additional flexibility by allowing specific requests to bypass WAF
inspection at the rule, rule group, or managed ruleset level. Exceptions can be
defined using request URI, remote IP address, or request header name and value,
helping customers tune WAF policies more precisely while keeping other
protections active. To configure exceptions, navigate to your WAF policy in the Azure portal, select Managed
rules, and then add an exception. Learn more: Application
Gateway documentation Front
Door documentation
items.title: Generally Available: Exceptions in WAF for Azure Application Gateway and Azure Front Door

items.description: Azure Site Recovery (ASR) now supports disaster recovery for Azure ARC-enabled Windows VMWare virtual machines and on-premise physical servers. Customers can protect ARC-managed machines with ASR while continuing to use Azure ARC for governance, inventory, monitoring and management capabilities. Learn more.
items.title: Generally Available: Azure Site Recovery Support for Azure ARC-enabled Windows VMWare/Physical servers

items.description: Automatic zone balance for Virtual Machine Scale Sets is now generally available. This feature continuously monitors scale sets deployed across availability zones and automatically redistributes VM instances when zonal imbalances occur. This helps reduce the risk that a single-zone outage disproportionately affects an application.Automatic zone balance uses a create-before-delete approach: Azure creates a replacement VM in an under-provisioned zone and validates its health before removing an instance from an over-provisioned zone. Built-in safeguards respect instance protection policies, coordinate with Azure Autoscale, avoid active or recently completed scale-set operations, apply cooldown periods, and replace only one VM at a time. This capability is best suited for stateless workloads and requires at least two availability zones, zonal instances, and application health monitoring. It can be enabled through the Azure portal, Azure CLI, PowerShell, or REST API.Learn more.
items.title: Generally Availabile: Automatic zone balance for Virtual Machine Scale Sets

items.description: Hardware Audit Logging for Azure Cloud HSM provides hardware-generated audit records for supported HSM management operations, helping organizations strengthen security monitoring, compliance reporting, governance, and forensic investigations. Customers can access human-readable records alongside HSM-signed binary audit data, signatures, and certificates to independently verify the authenticity and integrity of signed audit batches. Audit events are delivered to Azure Monitor Log Analytics for use in existing monitoring and investigation workflows.
items.title: Generally Available: Azure Cloud HSM hardware audit logging

Schedule incremental transfers to maintain secondary copies that can support business continuity scenarios, copy data across regions, consolidate file shares, or place data closer to applications and analytics workloads. Centralized scheduling, monitoring, auditing, and metadata preservation provide a managed approach to recurring file share copy operations.Azure Files-to-Azure Files data copy is now in preview for SMB shares. Sign up here.For questions or feedback, please reach out to the team at azurefiles@microsoft.com Learn more:Get started with Azure Files-to-Azure Files data copy in Azure Storage Mover (preview)Introduction to Azure Storage Mover
items.title: Public Preview: Azure Files cross-region data copy and synchronization with Azure Storage Mover

items.description:
Private network gateway for Azure Databricks is
now in Public Preview, enabling serverless compute to connect to resources in
your virtual network (VNet) and transitively connected networks through a
single managed gateway. Customers can use the gateway to access multiple
private resources, route serverless egress through their own firewalls or
network security appliances, and use stable, identifiable source IP addresses. This simplifies secure connectivity for
serverless workloads while giving organizations greater control over network
traffic and access to private resources. Private network gateway integrates with existing network
connectivity configurations (NCCs) and complements Azure Private Link,
providing additional flexibility for securing serverless network connectivity. Learn
more.
items.title: Public Preview: Azure Databricks Private network gateway
